questions_and_answers.question_text: How is nǎli translated as a reply to a compliment?
What has traditionally been considered proper in China on receiving a compliment?
Why do many people regard xièxie as an immodest reply to a compliment?
Which word for "only" is more widely understood than jiù?
Write the Chinese reply meaning "Not at all, not at all. I can speak only a little."

answers.answer_text: Nǎli, nǎli. Wǒ jiù huì shuō yìdiǎn.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Rewrite Wǒ jiù huì shuō yìdiǎn using the more widely understood word for "only."
Write the Chinese compliment meaning "Your Chinese is very good."
Does it matter how much truth there is in the compliment?

answers.answer_text: No — traditionally it has been proper and a matter of course to deny any compliment received, no matter how much truth there is to it.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which earlier unit already discussed jiù meaning "only"?

answers.answer_text: Unit 3, in the notes on Nos. 8-9.

articles.text:
9. A: Nǐde Zhōngguo huà hěn hǎo.            Your Chinese is very good.
   B: Nǎli, nǎli. Wǒ jiù huì                Not at all, not at all. I can
      shuō yìdiǎn.                          speak only a little.

Notes on No. 9

Literally, nǎli means "where." As a reply to a compliment, we have translated nǎli as "not at all." In China, it has traditionally been considered proper and a matter of course to deny any compliment received, no matter how much truth there is to it. Many people still regard xièxie, "thank you," as an immodest reply to a compliment, since that would amount to agreeing that the compliment was completely correct.

Jiù, "only": As was noted in Unit 3, notes on Nos. 8-9, jiù meaning "only" is not as widely understood as zhǐ. The last sentence in exchange 9 could just as well be Wǒ zhǐ huì shuō yìdiǎn.
